**Novelty (originality, unexpectedness): 4**
Why? The solution reframes resilience and ethical sourcing not as competing trade-offs, but as a single "visibility-and-relationship problem." The framing of "We do not buy parts. We buy the continued ability of a specific site, with specific people, to make them" is a striking conceptual shift. Furthermore, the "Time-to-Survive minus Time-to-Recover" (TTS - TTR) metric is a highly original, pragmatic analytical tool that bypasses the often-futile attempt to predict the probability of specific disruptions. 

**Usefulness/Feasibility (practicality, implementability): 5**
Why? The proposal is exceptionally grounded in corporate reality. It provides illustrative budgets, clear 90-day diagnostic timelines, and specific ROI expectations (18–30 months). It anticipates internal resistance (e.g., Operations viewing buffer inventory as a working-capital fight) and suggests pre-meeting strategies to secure buy-in. The governance structure is deliberately kept lean (two people, 45-minute meetings) to avoid bureaucratic bloat, making it highly actionable.

**Flexibility (multiple approaches, adaptability): 5**
Why? The solution explicitly rejects a one-size-fits-all approach. It uses a Kraljic-style segmentation matrix to tailor specific resilience and ethical treatments to different supplier categories (Strategic, Bottleneck, Leverage, Routine). It also offers a diverse menu of sourcing strategies (dual-sourcing, dormant alternates, capacity reservation, nearshoring) and acknowledges the specific scenarios where each is appropriate, allowing the company to adapt the framework to individual components.

**Elaboration (detail, development): 5**
Why? The level of detail is outstanding. The solution goes beyond high-level strategy to define specific data collection instruments, assign departmental ownership, and set hard deadlines (e.g., Day 30, Day 60). It even includes nuanced details like the "token order" to keep dormant alternates warm, and the insight that worker-voice tooling is 15% of the cost of an audit but finds more. *(Note: The text cuts off at section 5.2, but the elaboration up to that point is remarkably thorough).*

**Cultural Sensitivity (cross-cultural appropriateness): 4**
Why? The proposal demonstrates strong cultural and geopolitical awareness. It acknowledges that sub-tier suppliers will withhold data for "commercial reasons that are entirely legitimate from where they sit," showing empathy for differing business cultures. It also highlights specific international regulatory environments (UFLPA, CSDDD, EUDR) and addresses labor abuse risks like migrant labor intensity and recruitment agency practices. It misses a perfect score only because it focuses slightly more on Western corporate compliance than on proactive, localized community engagement in the sourcing countries.
